speechtext: I might say to the right hon. gentleman that in recent years a practice has grown up which is wholly at variance with what was the custom in this house or is the custom in the British House of Commons. To refer measures to select standing committees was not done with respect to all the great measures passed between 1806 and 1911, 1011 and 1917, and from 1920 forward. From time immemorial the Bank Act has been referred to a special committee for reasons that are obvious. But general legislation, upon which the government has determined its policy, is usually submitted to a committee of the whole house. I know of no reason why this measure should not be dealt with by a committee of the whole house, so that questions may be asked by hon. members and answers given by the minister in charge. If there are any good reasons given why this practice should not be followed, then those reasons will have to be considered and a conclusion arrived at in an endeavour to suit the convenience of the house and the best interests of the country as affected by the legislation. At the moment I can see no reason why this measure should follow other than the ordinary course, namely to be considered by a committee of the whole house after it has received second reading.

Mr. Speaker, the bill to which the house is asked to give second reading is the only measure the government has introduced thus far this session with respect to the relief of unemployment and farm relief, which continues to be the largest question before the country. The bill, as is apparent from its provisions, and as was stated at the time the resolution on which it was based was introduced, is similar to the measure which was enacted at the last session of parliament, the provisions of whic-h measure, however, expire on the thirty-first of this month.
I wish on the second reading to protest again as I did on the introduction of the resolution, against the little time that has been afforded the House of Commons for a discussion of this all-important question. As is well known, the house is to adjourn on Wednesday of this week and it was only on Thursday of last week that the resolution on which this bill is based was introduced. It is to-day, Monday, that we are asked to consider the second reading. After the second reading we shall have to discuss the bill at some length in committee and in order to become law before the Easter recess it has still to pass the Senate and receive the royal assent. If it does not become law before then, the position will be this, that though parliament has been in session now for a couple of months no provision of any kind will have been made with respect to the further relief of unemployment and for the relief of rural distress. In addition to that the government will be powerless to do anything whatever until some enactment is passed to enable it to deal with distress either in rural or urban areas, for the measure that was passed last session and which gives the government power when parliament was not in session to pass by order in council certain measures with respect to relief under the broad heading of peace, order and good government expires on the last day of this month. Moreover no supply for unemployment relief has as yet been voted. The act of last session gave the government moneys up to a certain sum for the purpose of unemployment relief; any portion of that sum ceases to be available with the expiration of the act, and the government will not have at its disposal any other moneys appropriated by this parliament for the purpose of unemployment relief. Nothing could show more clearly the indifference or neglect of the government or its incapacity to deal with this great question of unemployment than the fact that it is 74726-115
possible that this parliament may adjourn in the course of another two days with no legislation whatever enacted which will enable it to do aught for the relief of unemployment.
But serious as that is with regard to the immediate situation, it will be seen to become infinitely more serious when I draw attention to the fact that this delay in bringing down legislation relating to labour problems, and the problem of unemployment relief in particular, appears to be a deliberate policy on the part of the administration. It is the policy which has been pursued from the very beginning of the present parliament, to limit as much as possible any discussion in this house with respect to this great question of unemployment relief. Take the first session, the special session, called for the purpose of dealing specifically with the question of unemployment. Although hon. members came from all parts of the country to be present ait that session, the time occupied in discussing relief measures was only fractional as compared with the time taken up in the discussion of matters pertaining to the tariff, and amendments to the National Revenue Act. The session might much better have been termed a session to increase the tariff and give certain arbitrary powers to the Minister of National Revenue, than a session to deal with unemployment. The session of 1931 enacted the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931; the resolution under which that bill was introduced was not taken up until July 27; prorogation took place on August 3. Take the next session, that of 1932, which enacted two relief measures. The first of these, the Unemployment and Farm Relief Continuance Act of 1932, was not enacted until some time after the act of 1931 had expired. It continued its provisions from March 1 to May 1. It was April 26 before the Relief Act of 1932 was introduced, as I say. The Relief Act of 1932 was not introduced into the house until April 26, although the Unemployment and Farm Relief Continuance Act, passed earlier in 1932, expired on the first of May. That meant that in order to have the discussion over before the expiration again of the previous legislation dealing with unemployment matters the only other time the house was given to discuss the whole question of unemployment relief that year was between April 26 and May 1. As a matter of fact the bill did not pass the commons till May 12. Prorogation took place on May 26. The same thing happened in the session of 1932-33. If people wish to know why it is that they have had to pay a tax on sugar, if they wish to know why it is that the income tax has been increased, if they wish to know why it is that the sales tax and other taxes have been increased, they will find one of the reasons in the report of the auditor general which tells exactly how relief moneys have been spent by this government under the blank cheque authority which the government has sought and obtained from its followers.
I should like to refer to what was said in this house in 1930 when the government started this policy of contributing vast sums with no provision for a satisfactory audit. I should like to quote from Hansard of 1930, page 164. Speaking to the Prime Minister, I said:
If there is one time above another when the government should be careful to safeguard expenditures and to prevent extravagance and waste it is when this parliament is trying, with public money, to end unemployment and to use every cent to the advantage of those who are unemployed. How can we depart from a fixed principle, that principle being that this parliament must provide machinery for the audit of public expenditures, but that it cannot follow to its destination every expenditure that is made, involving an interference with the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures and municipal councils and bodies of that character. Are we to be told, because two or three members of this house stand up and complain of a provincial legislature, that therefore we are to insult that legislature by saying that we are to deal with their affairs and not our own? Are we to mind our business or their business?
Again, as reported on page 175, the Prime Minister had this to say:
I will look further into the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition, but I cannot conceive ho\v under our constitution any self-respecting province would expect the dominion government to place upon it what I regard as an unenviable and unnecessary insult by saying:

"Where any moneys are expended' under this act by way of contribution to provinces, municipalities, or other bodies, the auditor general shall audit the expenditure made by the province, municipality or other body, and shall report thereon to parliament within thirty days after the commencement of the next session."

This parliament has no jurisdiction to interfere with the provinces and the municipalities in the expenditure of their moneys. If that were made a condition I think it would be regarded by the provinces as an insult.
After four years, and after we have had this waste of public money that the auditor general has brought to the attention of the government, we have passed this order in council of March 12, 1934. Simply that the government may have something to point to, to enable it to say that it has taken a step to audit the accounts in a way which will safeguard the public treasury, and this after it is too late. This is done after, as I said the other day, it has become a physical impossibility for the auditor general to attempt, even with a staff as large as an army, to begin to find out how those moneys have been spent. I want to read the directions of this order in council again on top of what I have just given to the house:
Now therefore His Excellency the Governor General in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Labour, is pleased in the exercise of the powers so conferred by the Relief Act, 1933, to order and doth hereby order and direct the auditor general to conduct such audit of provincial and municipal accounts in connection with unemployment relief expenditures as he deems essential to safeguard the interests of the dominion treasury.
If it is possible to do that in 1934, surely it was possible to do it in 1930, in 1931, in 1932 and in 1933. The way in which this government has wasted the public money on unemployment relief is shocking beyond all words. We have only an indication there of the kind of thing that will be disclosed once there comes, as there certainly will in the course of time, a very full inquiry into the way in which those public moneys have been used. The point I wish to stress at the moment is that with this information before us, surely the house is not going to give to this administration power to issue from the public treasury

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Mackenzie King
any funds it pleases under a blank cheque given by the House of Commons: and that particularly, as I have already said, in a year in which there is likely to be a general election.
But those are not the only features of the bill which are bad. It has all the reprehensible features of the previous legislation but it has something reprehensible in addition that was in none of the other acts. We are being asked not only to give the government blanket authority to legislate with respect to peace, order and good government and to give them a blank cheque, but to give them the right to enter into commitments that will extend over a term of years. In other words they are asking for authority to make contracts in connection with public works and buildings and to commit the country to the expenditures involved not merely for the period of the next fiscal year but for a series of years thereafter. That, again, is wholly subversive of the rights of the House of Commons in its control of expenditure of public moneys and of its duty in the protection of the public in the matter of taxation. That clause should be struck out and I hope, when the bill comes into committee, the minister will see his way to do so, because he cannot begin to defend it.
In connection with this relief legislation, every single canon that exists with respect to the control by parliament over expenditure of public money has been violated, and set at naught by hon. gentlemen opposite. That wrong is being repeated in the bill before us. In the first place, by asking for this blanket authority to legislate and to spend, they are taking away from parliament altogether its functions in the appropriation of public moneys. Where they have come to parliament and asked for moneys, they have not brought in an estimate or given to the house any grounds on which an estimate might be based; they have not limited their appropriations to specific and definite items which, as no one knows better than does the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), is the proper way to proceed in asking the House of Commons for moneys for any purpose. Those principles have all been set at naught. In the face of results which we now can see were inevitable, we are being asked to repeat the same kind of action for another year. I do hope the house will pause before it allows the measure to pass in the form in which it is at present.
I want to make a further reference to the significance of these powers being asked for this year. From the beginning I said that I did not believe the government's idea was
primarily that of meeting the unemployment situation as an emergency, that its desire was simply to get power to deal with an emergent situation. I said that I thought they had rather in view what would serve the large financial corporations and the situation with which they would be faced when a general election came on. I think one has only to look at the list of the different uses to which the moneys voted under relief measures have been placed to see how true the statement is that for every dollar there has been spent and gone to labour for unemployment relief, a much larger sum has been spent or guaranteed in the interest of some financial corporation. Under this relief measure the government took power first of all to fix arbitrary values of securities held by insurance companies. What has that to do with the relief of unemployment? Yet it is under this broad power to pass orders in council with respect to peace, order and good government assumedly for the purpose of relieving unemployment that action has been taken. The government has advanced moneys to the provinces, a proceeding which of course was quite right, but in that case we should have had a bill introduced especially for that purpose and the agreements with the provinces should have been placed before parliament for its approval. The government has advanced money to Newfoundland under this measure. How can the government justify the advance of money to Newfoundland under a measure enacted by parliament for the purpose of affording relief to the unemployed?

What I have to say of that message is that the time to have called mass meetings to protest against arbitrary action on the part of the executive was four years ago when we, of the Liberal opposition in this house sought to arouse public opinion concerning action calculated to divest parliament of its powers of legislation and of the control of public moneys. For four years we have been steadily protesting against parliament being robbed of its authority in the matter of legislation and of the control of expenditures and taxation. Now when a provincial government undertakes to assume certain exclusive powers to meet a definite situation immediately a mass meeting is called to protest against an act of that kind. My reply to that message was that if there had been an infraction of provincial rights which demanded intervention it was the duty of the government of the day to intervene, that the leader of the opposition in the dominion parliament had no authority whatever to intervene in any provincial matter, and as far as he was true to the traditions of Liberalism in connection with relations between the provinces and the dominion he would allow the prov-

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Mackenzie King
inces to manage their own affairs and not attempt to intervene in them one way or another.
But what I want to ask is, what is going to become of our country if the government of one province after the other, in addition to the dominion government, undertakes to establish some form of complete control over public moneys and the right to deal with public resources as it thinks best? I deem it important to direct the attention of the house to what I regard as a very serious situation, namely that the example which has been set by this federal government and followed during the past few years has been such as to occasion provincial governments to adopt a like course. We have now at least two of them, and undoubtedly there will be more in the course of a little time-the same, I believe, is true of the government of Saskatchewan-making three up to the present, all beginning to emulate this government in the matter of taking away from parliament, in this case the legislative assembly, powers intended by the constitution to safeguard the rights and liberties and moneys of the people.

Well, that my hon. friend will have to judge for himself. What I do say is that once the public becomes accustomed to a certain method of procedure the seriousness of it ceases to be as apparent as it otherwise would be. I well remember that when this legislation was first introduced in this house hon. members were aghast, even hon. gentlemen opposite, and would not have countenanced it for one moment except that they believed there was an emergency which might be very serious, and which after all might only last a very short time. They were prepared to grant these emergency powers for one year, then they granted them for a second year, then for a third year, and for a fourth. What at first was given only to meet an emergency has come now to be a regular practice. Having come to be a regular practice by this government, it has come in virtue of its action and example to be assumed by provincial governments that such is the way they also should proceed to deal with their problems at this time. I say that raises the largest question that has ever been raised in this country. After all, Canada and other parts of the British Empire remain in the world to-day the one stronghold of the liberties of the people preserved by their parliaments and legislatures. If this country
begins to go as Europe has gone, and Asia has gone, and some other parts of the world appear to be going, what is going to happen to the rights and liberties and freedom of the people of Canada? I direct attention to that large issue at this time because I think it needs to be reemphasized- I raise it in connection with this legislation because it comes concretely before us in that connection.
Apart from all that, I say about the proposed enactment itself, that it does not contain one single line of a constructive policy. The relief measure suggested is a continuance of the dole, that is all in the way of policy the government has to offer, notwithstanding that it came into office on the promise that it was going to relieve unemployment and give work, not doles, to everyone who was ready and willing to work. So, Mr. Speaker, while we are not going to take exception to the second reading, which approves of the principle of giving relief where relief is a necessity, we will reserve to ourselves the right to ask the government to amend some of the clauses of this bill before it gets through the committee stage.
I want to say just this further word. While the legislation before us offers nothing but a continuance of the dole as a means of coping with the problem of unemployment, here when we have come to the fifth session of this parliament there is nothing of record as to what really has been achieved by the administration except this statement that $110,000,000 has been spent, and another $52,000,000 advanced in loans or guarantees and that, by the way, obviously does not include the $60,000,000 guarantee to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. There has been no national policy of any kind with respect to relief; there has been no national recovery plan. No commission, not even a department of government, has been gathering data that would have been of infinite service to parliament in dealing with the situation today, and in dealing with the unemployment insurance problem which will have to be dealt with in the future. There has been nothing but this vast expenditure, and the vast waste which I have quoted from the reports of the auditor general.

speechtext:
In his concluding words, Mr. Speaker, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) pointed out that this relief measure is a continuance of the dole. At this stage might I ask why, after almost four years of Conservative government, it should be necessary to bring in a relief measure. I think this is an appropriate time to ask what
182S

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Heenan
this government has done, if anything, towards eliminating the problem of unemployment. We all know that several factors contribute to employment. I think it will be agreed that one great factor is international trade; if we have international trade and our factories are working, men are employed instead of unemployed. Another great factor is the purchasing power of the people. If men earn wages and have money to spend they can do much to relieve unemployment. If the purchasing power of the people, however, is reduced by wages being lowered or by high taxation, so that men have very little to spend, the unemployment situation is only aggravated in this or any other country.
In examining the record of this government of necessity we must compare it with the record of the government which it displaced in 1930. I need not remind the house that during the regime of the Liberal government the trade of Canada gradually increased until in 1929 it amounted to $2,654,000,000, in round figures; that between 1926 and 1930 the Liberal government reduced the national debt of Canada to the extent of about $250,000,000, and that during the same time it reduced taxation at the rate of about $118,000,000 annually. Under the regime of the late government we had the largest number of persons employed in Canada since confederation, and those workers received the highest wages ever paid to workers in this country during peace times. The working population, with increased wages and therefore with increased purchasing power, were enabled to maintain a fairly high standard of living and in turn that enabled the railways to show surpluses instead of deficits and to increase the wages of their employees.
That was the state of affairs at the end of 1929, when the world depression set in. In comparison with other countries Canada stood up well under that depression. We had an election in 1930, however, and the leader of the Conservative party and his friends wanted power. They took the opportunity to go through this country and tell the people that they never had seen anything like the unemployment that existed at that time. According to their own figures after they came into office there were 117,000 people in Canada unemployed. The Conservative candidates, led by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), went through the country making rash statements which they must have known, if they knew anything, were not true; they made rash promises which, if they knew anything, they must have known they could not fulfil and which they never intended to fulfil. They stated that the unemployment prevailing at

the time was not because of world conditions but was because of the policies of the government that was in office at the time. They said it was the duty of the federal government to provide work for all the inhabitants of this country, and the right hon. gentleman said he would end unemployment or perish in the attempt. He made his position very clear at Sarnia, when he said:
Someone is responsible for unemployment; not individuals, but governments. Governments by their majorities in parliament are responsible for enacting all legislation.
In Quebec he said that if his party were returned to power and he did not fulfil his promises he wanted his followers from Quebec and the rest of Canada to vote him out of power. His words will be found in the Ottawa Citizen of July 14, 1930, and are as follows:
There was no necessity for a conference on unemployment, he continued. The solution was too apparent. "What you want is work," he exclaimed, " not conferences, and you are going to get work." Unless hiis promises to the people of Canada were kept if elected to office, Mr. Bennett said he wanted Quebec and other members of his party to vote Mm out of office.
"Wages, not charity" was the slogan of the right hon. gentleman on that occasion, and many thousands of workers throughout Canada took him at his word. They have had very little but charity since that time, and now we have before us a bill providing for an extension of the dole. Thousands of workers throughout Canada took the word of the right hon. gentleman and his candidates; they voted for a change of government, and they brought about that change. What has been the result of about four years of inactivity on the part of this government? No one will deny that conditions have been going from bad to worse; not even members sitting on the government benches will deny that statement. They make excuses, however. In 1929 the total trade of Canada in round figures was valued at $2,654,000,000. By 1933 the total trade stood at $886,000,000, representing a loss in trade between the years 1929 and 1933 of $1,768,000,000. Is it any wonder that we have unemployment? As a result of unemployment and the accompanying loss of wages there has been a reduction in the purchasing power of thousands of our citizens. The loss of salaries and wages in our industries is a distinct menace.
Let us consider the manufacturing industries. In 1930 the salaries and wages were $736,000,000. In 1932 they had dropped to $497,000,000, representing a loss in that respect alone of $239,000,000. That means that there Was $239,000,000 less purchasing power in Canada. Is it any wonder that our workers

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Heenan
are becoming depressed and dissatisfied? Is it any wonder that they are becoming impatient at the inactivities of the government, a government which upon assuming office found only 117,000 unemployed, but deplored the fact throughout the country? Last winter the Minister of Labour admitted that there were 1,357,000 persons on direct relief, and now, only about four years after the government took office, there are about half a million unemployed, and thousands more are working in relief camps for their board and miserable pittances.
What about the farmers? Are they content?-because I understand this is also a farm relief bill. After four years of this government's legislation should the farmers have to read in the newspapers that they must accept further relief? What were they promised by this government? This is a sample of what was told the farmers during the election campaign of 1930. The right hon. leader of the opposition of that day, the present Prime Minister, is quoted as follows in the Vancouver Province of June 18, 1930:
If Mr. Mackenzie King thinks I will not so build up our agricultural and industrial life, that its strength will drive our products into the markets of the world', then he is wrong, for that I will do. If he thinks I will not establish new markets for those products, strive with all my heart to retain them, drive our products with all my power into new markets, into old markets, into reluctant markets, he is wrong, for that I will do.
He meant it, all right, there can be no doubt about that, because he is quoted in the Montreal Gazette of June 19, 1930, as follows:
So will I, when the government is mine, continue to blast a way through all our troubles and difficulties.
Well, let us see how the farmers are faring at the present time. In January, 1930, the index figure of price levels for farm products stood at 102-6. In January, 1934, it had dropped to 55-3. For the year 1930 the index price level for farm products averaged 82-3; in 1933 it averaged 51.
Then the presentation on behalf of the farmers before the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada is found at page 70 of the report of the Macmillan commission:
In a memorandum prepared by a committee representing the governments of the three provinces . . .
The western provinces-

speechtext:
If I had them I would not have spread them on the record, because I am talking about Canada and not about the United States. It was a very high price for the railroad men of this country to pay- $243,000,000 less in wages and salaries in three years-for putting in power a government that advocates and puts into effect policies that tend toward a restriction of trade. If my hon. friend wants to compare the United States and Canadian railroads, I can tell him that so far as Canada's railways are concerned the number of railway employees in this country decreased by 65,000 in 1933 as compared with 1929. That is not ending unemployment. This government is simply adding to the hordes of unemployed, and apparently now the government has made up its mind that there will be no further necessity for many of the railroads in this country. The government has given up hope that they will ever get much of this lost trade back, because last year they passed the most iniquitous piece of legislation that was ever put over on a people in a white man's country. It was camouflage, because it resulted in the amalgamation of the operations of the railroads of Canada and in a pooling and merging of their services under the guise of cooperation. The purpose of this legislation was to eliminate duplication and certain main lines and branch line services. So it is quite evident that this government

Relief Act, 1984-Mr. Heenan
has made up its mind that we shall no longer require railroads to the same extent that we did previously. I say that that legislation was iniquitous because a direct pledge was given to the people by the present Prime Minister, standing in the centre of Canada on June 9, 1930, when he pledged himself and his party that the policy of his government with respect to the railroads would be "amalgamation never, competition ever". Before many years have gone by, Mr. Speaker, the words of warning I have given will be found to be only too true. Competition? It is not competition that we are getting on the railways. The present. Prime Minister must have known the conditions of the railroads at that time. He was not a young and green member of this house. He had been in parliament for years and had taken part in the debates on railway matters. I recall the time in this house, I think it was in 1913 or 1;914, when he designated the present leader of the government in the Senate as the gramophone of Mackenzie and Mann. So he was well versed in the railway situation at the time he was speaking. He it wa9 who stated at Winnipeg on June 9, 1930, "We are all proud of this nationally owned system. We are proud of the transportation system of Canada." And he also said during that campaign, speaking, as he said, to one million of his fellow countrymen over the radio, "If any of you hear or see me tampering with the railroads, ask for my resignation, because I shall be unworthy of the great position to which I aspire." Then lo and behold! we find that we have an amalgamation of the railways under the guise of cooperation. We find that there has taken place a pooling of passenger and freight traffic, and that about ninety railway men have been laid off by the pooling of services between Ottawa and Toronto. The Minister of Railways, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) the other day, stated that ninety-six men were affected between Quebec and Montreal. When he was reading a letter he had received from the chairman of the board of trustees he said that these ninety-six men would not lose their positions; apparently he was trying to leave the impression that they would just revert to other jobs by virtue of their seniority. Everyone knows that these ninety-six men engaged in passenger service would not lose their jobs; they would find work in mixed or freight service, but they would push ninety-six other men off the bottom of the list. Men who have been twenty and twenty-five years in the railway service, and who have worked them-74726-116
selves up to be engineers and conductors, cannot get jobs to-day as wipers or brakemen.
This measure states that further relief is needed by the provinces. I wonder if the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) have looked up the public works estimates from 1930 down to the present. Those estimates show a continuous reduction in the amounts voted for public works. Public works would have furnished relief to the unemployed in the various provinces. During the elections of 1930 this government promised that they would construct a great national highway with funds from the federal treasury, and that they would administer old age pensions from the federal exchequer. They promised also that they would provide for technical educational training, and in 1931 passed a bill under which an annual payment of $750,000 was to be made for fifteen years. Had those payments for technical education been made, a total of $2,250,000 would have been paid to the provinces down to the present time.
After listening to the speech of my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) one can understand why there is such a small amount left with which to pay the wages of the working men of this country. I may have something to say about this in the future. This government permits the governments of Ontario and other provinces to pay starvation wages under the guise of unemployment relief at a time when they are contributing one-half the cost. Why they have nothing to say about this is beyond me. This bill gives the government full power to make regulations with respect to the matter. When the subject was first before the house in 1930 the government made the promise that the fair wage and eight hour day clauses would apply to these works. According to the regulations which I have before me the provincial governments are permitted to set a maximum wage, that is, the government receiving money shall not pay more than what is paid by the federal government for the same class of work. The provincial government may pay as small a wage as they want to as long as they do not pay a wage higher than that paid by the federal government. This is a reversal of the whole fair wage policy; it allows a maximum wage instead of a minimum wage.
Having regard to the fact that we have a Conservative government in power; that this government has destroyed the trade of Canada; that this government has apparently given up all hope of recovering that trade; that this government led the way in the re-



Reliej Act, 1934-Mr. Nicholson
duction of wages and seemed to be proud of having done so, I suppose we should be very thankful even for this bill. Perhaps we should get up and thank the Minister of Labour and the government on behalf of the workers of Canada for allowing them to live. All I can see in this bill is the giving of a pittance to the workers to keep them from hungering to death. I can speak with knowledge on this matter because during last fall I visited some of these men. I saw the conditions in their homes. I have seen sickness and death in the homes of men who were working on the highways in northern Ontario. I have seen a hat passed around to buy a casket. I do not want to shed crocodile tears and try to make things out to be worse than they are. Whatever this government may give to the provincial governments, to the municipalities or to any other body, they should act according to the wish of this house, and it is the expressed wish of this house that fair wages should be paid on all works constructed by means of contributions, grants or guarantees from the federal government. With the exceptions as expressed by my right hon. leader, I support this bill.

subtopic: BILL IN TERMS GENERALLY OF RELIEF ACT, 1933, WITH PROVISION RESPECTING DELAYED RELIEF ACCOUNTS

Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house, although not the most important one that will come before us this session, at least deals with what I conceive to be the most difficult problem confronting the Canadian people, namely, that of taking care of those who, by reason of unemployment, are unable to take care of themselves. More particularly is this the case because of the difficulties with which those are beset who are endeavouring to get Canadian workingmen into employment where they can earn a living for themselves and their families.
I am not at the moment going to follow the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan), who preceded me immediately before six o'clock, excepting as regards one question. My hon. friend made a comparison of the attitude of the present government with regard to unemployment with that of the government of which he was a member prior to 1930. This reminded me very forcibly of a situation that developed in the part of the country with which I am more particularly acquainted, northern Ontario, when from a period quite early in 1929 there had
[Mr. Hpenan.l
been a serious unemployment situation in the pulp and paper industry arising out of the collapse in a large measure of that industry. The hon. member who preceded me as representative for East Algoma, the Hon. Mr. Bowman, came to Ottawa to intercede with the Minister of Labour of that day, to see whether he could arrange some plan whereby the federal Department of Labour would join with the government of Ontario in providing relief for the 389 families that were entirely destitute at Espanola. The delegation that was here to meet the then member for East Algoma had the pleasure of sitting in the gallery immediately above where I stand and watching the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, then Minister of Labour, pound his desk in ecstatic glee as his leader spat out the words: "Not a five cent piece" to relieve unemployment in Ontario.

At other times, however, he makes use of his position for political purposes to render it difficult for all those who directly or indirectly are endeavouring to provide employment for workingmen in Canada,
A few days ago, speaking in the house on this and kindred subjects, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette) made statements to which I shall refer in some little detail later on, but at the moment I wish to say that those statements were of a character that indicate one of two things, and the hon. members can take their choice. They were either speaking of something of which they knew absolutely nothing or deliberately misrepresenting the facts. I might put the situation more strongly than that, but I think that will indicate what I mean.
In an effort to relieve unemployment, to put men back to work, the governments of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia last year took steps to confer with operating lumbermen, pulp and paper manufacturers, to see what could be done, to take advantage of the opportunities presented in the United Kingdom market by

reason of the 1932 Ottawa agreements, and also of the apparent upturn in the pulp and paper industry to see what the operators could do in getting men into the woods. As the situation in Ontario had been specifically mentioned, I shall deal with that province alone because I happen to know something of conditions there. As nearly as it was possible to tell, every operator from the Ottawa river to the western boundary line adjoining Manitoba met together with the Minister of Lands and Forests and his officials in Toronto and discussed the problem for a full day. Arrangements were made under which a number of operators agreed to undertake certain operations that they felt then were justified in order to take men off relief in northern Ontario. When I give the house the story of what has happened in the meantime, it will have some appreciation of what I meant when I spoke of the difficulties facing those who were endeavouring to provide employment to men who were on unemployment relief. No sooner had those operations begun, no sooner had it been announced that certain firms, contractors and companies were arranging to put men into the bush, than a composite organization which can best be described as the federation of Canadian communists, began to take action to make it impossible for woods operations to be carried on. The difficulty arose first in the Port Arthur district; it later spread to what is termed northern Ontario in its most northern point along the transcontinental railway, Kapuskasing, Smooth Rock Falls, Cochrane, Iroquois Falls; then along the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario and later along the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway through the part of the country in which I live. As evidence of the character of the organization let me say that ten days before any employer of labour or woods operator in the Port Arthur district was advised by any man or organization that there was any difficulty whatsoever, a communist newspaper, the original editor of which, Arvo Vaara, was deported from this country, published in Sudbury a notice to bush workers throughout northern Ontario advising them that there were going to be strikes in the woods operations in that section and saying: "Woodsmen, keep away."

Yes, not once, but twice, at >my request, to see that the camps were in proper condition. I went to one camp, and I shall just give this as an illustration of the organized malingering. Fifty-two men were engaged in cutting pulpwood by the cord at a price ten per cent higher than that which is provided for under the N.R.A. code in the states of Michigan and Wisconsin and the northeastern part of the United States. That rate prevails both for monthly men and for piece workers all over northern Ontario, in the district represented by my hon. friend as well as that which I have the privilege of representing. These fifty-two men produced in one week 206 cords of pulpwood-a fair

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Nicholson
average but not up to normal. But when analysis was made of what the men actually did it was found that twenty-one of these men produced 162 cords and thirty-one produced 44 cords out of the 206. Half of the thirty-one men did not produce a cord of wood in a week. Thus it was made impossible for the contractor to operate, and he was defrauded of the money he had advanced for transportation, food and clothing for these men, to the extent that Brownlee Brothers are to-day out of pocket in actual cash in that regard between $6,000 and $7,000. I know it had exceeded $6,000 at the end of January;
I have not the figures for February or March up to date.
But that is not all. The communists work through these camps all the time. I have proof of the fact that when a group of men is put on the train by the employment service at Toronto, or when a group of men is put on at Sudbury, one or two communists get on the train with them and go into the camps. The camps are permeated with them. They continued this from the 30th October to the 15th of January. Then six communists, financed by Vapaus in Sudbury, secured tickets under false pretences, giving false names, from the government employment office and came to Brownlee Brothers' headquarters and were sent to the Jack Pine river on January 9. They hired as pulpwood cutters. They had never cut pulpwood in their lives, and so acknowledged; they knew nothing about it. They stated to travellers on the train that their purpose in going there was finally to tie up Brownlee's work, and bring about a strike if they could. It just happened that I was in the camps on that occasion; I did not know or see the men at that time, but I was there and I knew where these men went on their arrival that night. On January 15, I received a wire in Toronto that the men were leaving Brownlee's camps. I took the first train to Chapleau, from which point I went into the camps by plane to see what was the situation. I arrived on Tuesday, the sixteenth, and as I flew over the tote road I could see the men coming out.
Let me repeat that not a single man employed by Brownlee Brothers ever made any representation that he was dissatisfied with his wages or with the conditions under which he was living or working. After the men had left the camps, however, a series of demands was presented to Brownlee Brothers by a communist who had hired under the name of Riley. This man at times went under the name of Dacko, and as nearly as it is possible to learn his real name was Davis. He
was an ex-convict who had been out on ticket of leave for about a year; his leave had just elapsed. I am not going to take time to read these demands, which cover five pages, but I should like to quote one or two of them. One demand was that Brownlee Brothers undertake to secure the release of seven communists from Kingston penitentiary. Another was that they secure the repeal of section 98 of the criminal code, and another was that they undertake to recognize all workers' organizations, including the communist party. Finally they demanded that if the work were to be carried on in these camps the company had to undertake to agree to allow the workers' unity league, as it was called there, to organize camp committees, such committees to say where the men would work, how they would work, how the timber should be cut and so on, and no man was to be disciplined or removed without the consent of the committee. Let me say in passing, Mr. Speaker, that I have something, though not all, to do with Brownlee Brothers. When the time comes for the communists to say how the work is going to be carried on, then instead of using their funds to destroy industry in this country they will have to use their funds to finance industry.
It was stated, as my hon. friend has stated, that there was a strike. I say to you now, sir, and I know whereof I speak, that there never was a strike of any kind. Men were jumping, to use the expression used in the lumbering industry; they were walking out without saying why they were going or anything else. It is true that on January 15 and 16 these communists succeeded in getting a larger number to leave, but, as I say, they made no representations to their employers as to any changes they might desire. These communists were not employees of Brownlee Brothers in any sense whatever. They were there under false pretences, and if I had my way the law of this country would be changed in. order that these men could be put behind the bars, where they belong, for that sort of thing. Of a total of 561 men, 228 walked out. I had occasion to meet the men at their headquarters; I mingled with them, and I saw men whom I have known for years being led around by the nose by a group of men whose only purpose in this world is to destroy the opportunity for Canadian citizens to earn a living. One of the communists, who is now in gaol, had broken his parole in order to participate in this disorganization of industry in northern Ontario. He came out ahead of the men and came to the town of Chapleau. He had enough money to hire a large hotel;

The signature to this letter is authentic, and I believe it gives an answer to the innuendo made by the hon. member. Again I repeat, I am in favour of labour organizations in our lumber camps. I repeat the statement I made in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, that conditions existing in some of the camps were a disgrace to the Canadian nation. As far as the activities of communists are concerned, if any of these people attempted to get into any of these camps, they would be thrown out. The big newsprint mills at Ka-puskasing, Spruce Falls and Iroquois Falls have recognized the new union. These companies are ready to bargain with the men and they have bargained and cooperated on several occasions since the strike was settled. The men are receiving justice from the larger corporations. Since the strike was settled the Ontario and Quebec governments have found it possible to amend their labour laws so that the axemen and bushmen in our section of the country will receive better treatment than they have in the past. I do not intend to retract one word of what I have said on two previous occasions. As the hon. member has

made an attack upon me personally, when we get into committee I intend to give the whole history of the strike in the Austin and Nicholson camps in the Chapleau district.
Leaving this matter aside, I shall deal now at some length with a matter about which I have spoken on several occasions in previous years. The back to the land movement has a direct bearing upon the matter now before [DOT] the house. A large number of people now residing in my section of the country have come under this scheme. They have left the larger centres of population in old Ontario and have taken up land in the clay belt, particularly in the riding which I have the honour to represent. I intend to follow the course I followed in the past and not make any destructive criticism of the administration. I intend to speak as a tiller of the soil and as a pioneer in my section of the country. I shall refer to the many good things which have happened under this scheme. If the government are really sincere, they will see that it is enlarged. This was the attitude I took in the fall of 1930, because I realized it was a step in the right direction. The following year the government was boasting that this movement was a success, although they had not found it possible to spend any money upon it. I told the government at, the time that this movement would never 'be a success until more money was spent. Another movement was inaugurated the following year in a more concise form. By means of a tripartite agreement between the federal, provincial and municipal authorities, people were placed upon the land. This was an enlargement of the first scheme, and it promised more fruitful results. I am not going to go at any length into the details of that policy as it has been applied particularly in northern Ontario, but as a whole the back to the land movement has been a success. A few cases may be picked out; where men who have been following one type of occupation for ten, fifteen, twenty or twenty-five years are suddenly placed in new occupations in different centres of colonization, naturally some of them are found wanting and return to their previous locations. But generally speaking- and this applies particularly to every section of my riding-ninety per cent of the people placed in the baek to the land movement scheme of this government are making a success of their new calling. There are anomalies; no doubt the system is not perfect, but I am giving due credit to the provincial and federal authorities for their effort to remedy to some extent, within the limit of the scheme, some of the drawbacks that a new population has to face.
Last year I stated that I thought the provincial government should have a better follow-up policy, and last summer I am glad to say that more attention was given to those new centres of population. First of all the people were placed in more concentrated areas; they were placed, for instance, in the township of Kennedy south of my home town. At least sixty families were put along the same road where the land was carefully surveyed to allow those people to have access to the main highway and to be closer to one another. This is certainly a step in the right direction.
One matter that I want to bring to the attention of the house at this time is the fact that there is much resentment of the attitude taken by the provincial authorities in not rendering monthly accounts of the money those people are receiving from the government. No doubt the prices are correct, but they do not know what they are paying for their goods; they do not know what they have to pay for the material they put into their buildings, stables and so forth, or what prices they are charged for some of the equipment they have received from the government. When the federal government finds it possible to grant those people S600, that amount becomes their sole property and they are entitled to receive a statement of their purchases of the previous month, the same as anyone dealing with a store on a credit basis is entitled to receive a statement of the goods purchased during the previous month. I am bringing this to the attention of the government because it is a matter that is easily remedied. Apart from a few minor anomalies that I found more particularly two years ago -the fact, for instance that some people were placed on new holdings where there was no colonization road and where they had to pack on their backs and in some instances carry for several miles provisions for themselves, their families and their cattle-the situation is being remedied gradually. Last summer the Hon. Mr. Finlayson found it possible to visit most of those new centres of colonization, not only in my section but in the whole of northern Ontario. There is, however, one anomaly that exists, under the present scheme, and it is something which will test the sincerity of the government in regard to it. The back to the land policy has caught the attention of the whole of the Canadian people. It came at the proper time; it has been accentuated on account of the prevailing economic conditions. The movement holds great promise for the equilibrium of population between the urban and the rural

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Bradette
centres, but I state frankly and sincerely that the present scheme does not go far enough. One limitation I have in mind, and one that is practically at the root of the question of the present administration of this policy, is the fact that it is a tripartite scheme. There is a section of our population which will more readily settle on the land, the farmers' sons, the young people who have spent their youth on the farm. This I suppose applies to every rural section not only of Ontario but of Canada generally. These young people find it impossible under this scheme to receive the $600 offered by the three different governments. I maintain that if the federal government is sincere in regard to this policy it will enlarge it, making it purely provincial and federal, so as to apply to all who have the necessary qualifications who live in organized or unorganized districts, in little towns, not necessarily in cities. I have in mind at the moment a number of people in my section, and this will apply just as forcibly to the riding of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). Our rural families have a surplus population that cannot be absorbed on the land, for the very good reason that while a farmer may be able to place a son-the eldest or maybe another-if he has two, three or four left, on account of the present financial situation he cannot place them also. Most of the farmers, practically all of them, find it impossible to place all their sons on the land. But if the scheme were enlarged to apply to young people not only in my section, but in every rural section of Canada, so that the $600 would be within their reach, thousands instead of hundreds of people would be induced to settle on the land. This would be a step in the right direction, and one of the best ways of solving the unemployment problem.
In all these schemes it is always easy to use poetic terms, to speak of the fine population living on the farms, and to describe farming as an arcadian occupation, almost an idyll, but any hon. member who knows the hard work the farmer has to do and the length of time he has to wait for the results of his labour without any remuneration therefor will realize that farmers are not interested in poetical descriptions. They want something concrete, something substantial. They feel that the government should enlarge the scheme. They know that the solution of the agricultural, the rural problem, means the solution of all the ills confronting the country, because the source of a nation's vitality is its rural population and the basis of its economic prosperity is agriculture.

I want to make myself very clear. Although for the last three years I did not criticize the movement, and it is not my intention to do so at the present time, I believe the people want this government to prove their sincerity by enlarging their policy. Only a few days ago in the Ontario legislature the Hon. Mr. Pinlayson asked for the sum of $75,000 which will be required by the Ontario government to place 250 families on the land. Anyone ' familiar with the present unemployment situation realizes that to take only 200 or 250 families away from the urban centres and place them in rural districts is only a drop of water in the bucket; it is only a beginning in solving the problem. A few days ago the Minister of Labour said that in Ontario last year the sum of $25,000 was spent in the back to the land movement. Such a sum is simply ridiculous. The government, to show its sincerity in regard to this movement, should spend money not by the hundreds but by the hundreds of thousands of dollars.
There is a reason for the back to the land movement. Only a few days ago the Minister of Labour mentioned the fact that in the past we had a bad immigration policy. I am pleased to refer to that because some years ago when I was on the government side I deplored the attitude of the administration of that day towards immigration. A Canadian citizen is struck by the fact that most of the people who came here at that time had the idea of settling on the land. Although there was plenty of land available and the soil was fertile, because of the amount of capital required to farm ninety-five per cent of them found their way back into the cities. It was not so much the immigration policy that was wrong as the new social order we had to face. That trek of the rural population to the larger centres is not a new thing; you read of it in the history of countries like England,, France, Italy and Germany, for centuries past. This trek to the large centres was accentuated when industry, reaching its golden age of development, became more highly specialized and a working man received a fair remuneration and was in a position to have at hand some ready cash. I remember my grandfather saying on several occasions that there were years when they did not see any real money on the farm. The movement to the larger centres of population was accentuated also by the war. Many demobilized young soldiers, having tasted of the pleasures and the glamour of city life, were not content to go back to the old father and the old farm. And so it was with the younger people who remained in

Reliej Act, 1934-Mr. Bradette
Canada during the war, on account of the high wages they received in the munition factories. But now that the situation is so bad in the industrial centres; now that we have what is called technological unemployment, a displacement of labour in highly mechanized industries, we find people in the cities looking away beyond the confines of their habitat to the green fields of agricultural life. Most of those who want to go back to the land have had a certain amount of agricultural training. To-day we are talking of unemployment insurance, and it is coming; we hear of the four hour day and the five day week; they are coming. But the present conditions, instead of making for equilibrium between the city and the country, are intensifying the difficulties in that regard. When the wheels of industry return to normal operation many who have been placed on the land will return to the cities; many young sons of our farmers, will find their way to the larger centres, because the country people have not received and are not receiving the attention from the government that the industries have received through tax exemptions, tariff protection and various forms of municipal, provincial and federal aid. Our best brains have been applied to the assistance of industries; artificial means have been employed to help them, and, the result is that our rural centres of population are declining. That is true even of our new sections and of the whole of the western provinces. I well remember when as a young man I lived on the farm we had local industries- the wheelwright, the harness maker, the shoemaker, the grist mill, the woollen mill, the general store, and so on. These employed a good number of people, and as our requirements were limited and we were satisfied with less, the rural sections were practically selfsupporting. To-day the situation is absolutely changed. Anyone visting the famous clay belt of northern Ontario, one of the finest agricultural sections of Canada, sees these small villages with perhaps a little church, perhaps a blacksmith's shop, one or two stores, but practically no local industries, no hospital, no such local institutions as I have mentioned; everything is becoming more and more centralized in the larger centres. A few months ago I read with interest an article in the Ottawa Journal stating that industries were being decentralized. Well, perhaps in our day we shall see a miracle, but I for one am doubtful whether industry will find it possible to decentralize to such an extent as to bring back our rural centres to what they were thirty years ago. So we must adapt ourselves
to the new order. If in the past we had to employ artificial measures to build up what we call our modern industry, we must adopt similar measures to encourage people to remain on the farms, which are the mainstay of any country. If our rural people could get a reasonable price for their products; if for the last three years western Canada had sold wheat at a dollar a bushel, with a market for all their production, unemployment and depression would be unknown in Canada. Agriculture and industry are closely linked together; there is no section of the country that is not concerned about the labourer and the farmer. The industrialists of the east are just as much interested in the wheat crop as are the wheat growers of the west. It certainly is a step in the right direction, therefore, when we find the provincial governments and the central administration and every public body concerned about the state of the farmer and seeking a solution for his problems.
I make this appeal very sincerely, I say that the present scheme does not go far enough. An expenditure of $25,000 in one year on the back to the land movement to restore the equilibrium between the two sections of our population is ridiculous. There is now under way a movement looking to slum clearance, which has been greatly accelerated by Doctor Bruce, the lieutenant-governor of Ontario. It is true that there are slums in our larger centres of population but if one could see side by side some of the little dwelling houses and log shacks and tumbledown sheds, stables and barns that are scattered throughout our newer sections, he would know the exact meaning of the word "slum." The original settlers have not been able to graduate from the status of pioneers to that of farmers; they find it impossible to put up proper dwellings for their families. Sanitary conveniences are practically unknown through lack of funds. In all these small places you will find cleanliness, but the fact remains that the dwellings are not sanitary. There are no proper means of ventilation, and they are far too small in many cases to meet the needs. Here is a wonderful opportunity for the government to inaugurate a policy which, as well as doing away with slums in the larger centres, could be adapted to providing better housing conditions for the farmers. The appropriation of
S5.000.000 a year for twenty years to assist in providing better housing for the rural population would be one of the finest steps the government could take. In my section the settlers see new people come in among them, and they ask themselves the question: How is it that after we have toiled for fifteen or
Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Bradette

twenty years to develop this country, at a time when unemployment is just as pronounced in our midst as it is in the larger centres, the government finds it possible to give these people $600 per family while we who have done the initial work of colonization are left practically to ourselves?
The hon. member for East Algoma a few moments ago spoke of the great sacrifices the lumber dealers had to make last fall to give employment to the poor settlers. But I say it was sacrifice to the settlers to work under that scheme. In my own riding they were getting the magnificent sum of $3.50 a cord for pulpwood. No settler can keep body and soul together on returns as small as this. Something will have to be done. I do not doubt for a moment the sincerity of any hon. member on either side of the house, regardless of what the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Nicholson) said against me. Still less have I doubted the sincerity of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). I say that very sincerely. But we find to-day among our native rural population a certain amount of dissatisfaction because they seem to have been left out of the existing order of things. So far as this policy is concerned apparently they are the forgotten men. Because they happen to live in the newer sections of the country, in unorganized districts which have not enough money to come under this scheme, most of their young men cannot be placed on farms. I do not ask the government to lay out millions or tens of millions of dollars; for a few hundred thousand dollars it would be possible to maintain all the young men in our section of the country.
In passing may I say that in my opinion the educational system of our province has been wrong in its relation to the rural population, but there are signs of the application of remedy. To-day we have college graduates in northern Ontario who under this scheme would be good farmers. A man on the threshold of life in my section of the country finds only two courses open to him now. If he goes on the farm without assistance he sees ahead of him a drab life of near despair, with no hope of success, but if he could receive government assistance he would have a good chance to come through and live a fuller life. Assistance has been given our industries in the past, and that money has not been begrudged in my section of the country. I have a vivid recollection of the occasion that the government bonused the wheat growers, when millions were spent in the west; not a word of criticism was heard from my section of the country. Last year we set up a stabilization fund which we ex-

pected would cost us from $5,000,000 to $8,000,000. L>ue to the fact that the English pound came to parity with the Canadian dollar that money was not needed, but the fact remains that in my section of the country we were willing to have that money spent to help agriculture. Surely, then, it ought to be possible for the government to work out a scheme which will permit our rural population to remain at their present occupation. Farming is not a profession; it is not a trade. It is more than that; it is a vocation. Sometimes people are inclined to laugh and to ridicule the farmers, saying that they ask too much, that they are not content to live on the farms. It is said that they insist on the attractions of the city. The farming population have an absolute right to the comforts that exist in the cities, but they are willing to make certain sacrifices in order to remain on the land, because there is a great appeal in having their own farms. To them the farm is their kingdom, where they can maintain the traditions of their ancestors, whether they be from the great Loyalist stock of southern Ontario or from that of the pioneering Frenchman who colonized the shores of the St. Lawrence river. These people have it in their hearts to remain on their holdings, and they are the finest people we have in Canada. They are one of the greatest stabilizing factors in the nation, if not indeed, the greatest.
During the last ten years in eastern Canada, with the price of land going up and with industry attracting workers, the young people have found it impossible to remain on the land. The movement towards the cities will not be stopped until we find it possible to allow the young people to settle on the land. It is not my intention to dwell longer on that very important question, but I believe this offers the solution of the evils we have to face at the present time. Let me repeat that if to-morrow our farmers could receive a fair return for what they have to sell, to-morrow unemployment would disappear. We must remember that a farmer must be and is also a business man in the true sense of the word. Sometimes, because the farmers live so far apart, they have not the organization that exists in other industries, but the farmer is a business man, and the fact remains that no class invest their money more readily than do the farmers. A prosperous farmer seldom puts his money into a savings account; he reinvests it in better buildings, new equipment, or improved stock, and this should make the government realize the necessity of finding a solution for the rural problem. In French we say, " La

Relief Act, 1934-Mr. Plunkett
pitie de 1'agrieulture," speaking of his present plight, which is absolutely true. At present the farmers are toiling but are not receiving hardly anything in the way of remuneration; they realize that in the past they have not received the attention they deserve, and they are in a state of despair. Here we have a solution of the problem. Here lies the hope for the rural population of this country, its lifeblood, its future. Let us not lose sight of the fact that Canada must remain primarily a rural country. If we fail in this regard we shall suffer as all pasrt civilizations have when they allowed agriculture to deteriorate and decline.

Mr. Speaker, I am intensely interested in this unemployment and farm relief bill, and wish to make a few remarks in regard to it. I have the misfortune to represent a district which for the past five years has had no crop whatever. Of our people ninety-five per cent are on direct relief; ninety-five per cent have to receive their dole from the government each month. In regard to conditions in my constituency may I say that it is necessary for the farmers to haul their grain, straw, hay and rough feed from the towns out to the country so that they may feed their stock. No hay, straw, grain or rough feed of any kind have been grown there for the last five years. One may gather from that information an idea as to the conditions under which the people in that district have been living due to the crop failures in the past five years.
I do not wish to criticize the government with respect to the manner in which it has handed out unemployment and direct relief in my constituency. Politics has played no part in the handing out of relief, but I do offer criticism from a business standpoint, because in relief measures there has been an absolute lack of business practice. As the years go by and relief measures are continued the people in charge seem to become more and more inefficient, and each year more difficulties arise.
May I give an illustration of what took place in my own district. The people there were told that anyone living within twenty miles of the coal mines had to go to the mines to get coal. They were ready to comply with that arrangement, and were waiting for orders. They waited a long time, and time after time sent in requests for coal orders. At last, when winter weather had set in and coal was essential, they went to the coal miners and, almost on their knees, asked for coal. The coal miners replied, " We will give each of you a ton of coal, so as to carry you over, and when your orders come in let us have them." The people got their coal from the miners, but did not receive any orders until late in November when the snow was on the ground and frost had set in. Why those orders could not have been given

For some reason last fall the authorities took the notion that all orders for flour had to be for a particular brand; the order received indicated the type of flour which had to be purchased. One would think that an organization which had been handling relief measures for five years would be working smoothly by this time, but year by year they seem to be unable to meet the difficulties and get into more and more trouble.
As I have said, ninety-five per cent of the people in my constituency are ion 'relief. Let me indicate for the benefit of ban. members the amount of relief they receive. We have heard from many sources, Mr. Speaker, of the terrible problem that exists in this country with regard to our wheat. We have a great carry-over of wheat that we do not know what to do with. We want to get rid o'f it; why not put some of it to a useful purpose? Some have suggested that this wheat be sent to China to feed Chinamen. Charity begins at home. Why not use a little of it to help our own people? If I may suggest it to the government, why not take this wheat, mix it up with oats and barley and other grains, have it ground up into feed and give it to these farmers so that they may feed their stock? Finance them, if
you will. Do not give it to them, for they do not get relief to-day in any form whatever for nothing. The farmers have to sign notes for whatever they get from the relief commission; let them sign a note for the feed. Then they will have something to do; it will enable them to work for a living. They can start to feed poultry and pigs and sheep and other stock, and raise and sell this stock and make a living in that way. If this suggestion were acted upon, not only in the west but all over Canada, the government financing it, if you will, in a year's time or eighteen months, or at most two years, we would be able to supply our full quota of bacon and ham in the English market; there is no doubt about that, and our people would be doing something and earning a living. Besides we would be getting rid of this surplus glut of wheat of twenty or thirty or fifty million bushels. France has a scheme whereby she puts an analine dye in her wheat to make it unfit for use as flour. Why not in somewhat the same way grind our surplus wheat up with oats, barley and other grains so that it cannot be used for flour, and then hand it out to these people to be used as feed for their stock.
The whole morale of our people has gone. When you put people on the dole, on charity, and tell them to live on a handout from day to day, their whole morale goes. I have heard people say, "Oh, the morale of the west is as good as ever," but I do not find it so, I am sorry to say, and I believe it is due to the dole more than anything else.
I just want to leave that suggestion with the government. I believe it would be a good scheme to take some of our surplus grain and grind it up into feed and supply it to our farmers, financing the thing so that the farmers could earn a living for themselves and not have to be kept on the dole.
